ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geriatric Psychiatry Referral — Mark Twain

code.originalText: Establishing primary care a year after his wife's death: yearning, poor sleep, low mood and withdrawal, suicide risk, heavy cigar smoking, chest tightness on hills, gout and cardiovascular risk

text.paragraph: Persistent yearning, poor sleep, low mood and withdrawal a year after his wife's death in a 69-year-old writer who has also lost a son and a daughter, with passing thoughts of wishing to join her. Please assess for prolonged grief disorder and major depression, and advise on treatment, sleep and suicide risk. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the same day as his one-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Does he meet the DSM-5-TR criteria for prolonged grief disorder, and does he also have major depressive disorder?
Do you advise an antidepressant?
Which psychological treatment do you recommend, and how often?
How should we assess and manage his suicide risk, given his passive thoughts of death?
How should we treat his sleep at his age?
Is varenicline safe for him if he decides to stop smoking?

text.paragraph: Widowed a year ago after 34 years of marriage; his wife died after 22 months of illness. Earlier deaths of a son in early childhood and of his eldest daughter at 24. Since his wife's death he thinks of her many times a day, keeps her room as it was, avoids photographs of her, sleeps four to five hours, has stopped seeing friends and cannot finish any writing. PHQ-9 11 with item 9 scored 1: some days he wishes he could join her, with no intent, plan or past attempt; no firearms; a glass of whisky most evenings (AUDIT-C 3). Safety plan made and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline saved in his phone. About fifteen cigars a day since boyhood; gout with a urate of 8.6 mg/dL; exertional chest tightness under evaluation (ECG normal; CT coronary angiography booked). TSH and vitamin B12 normal; hemoglobin A1c 5.8 percent. No history of mania. He is witty and engaged when not speaking of her [S]

list.item: He says the year since his wife died has not softened anything, and he wants to be able to work and see his friends again. [S]
He does not want to give up cigars, which he says help him write, but worries about his heart. [S]
He wants the gout attacks to stop. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born on November 30, 1835, in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children; at four he moved with his family to Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River. [D]

Writing for a Virginia City, Nevada, newspaper, he first used the pen name Mark Twain; he became a celebrated writer, humorist and lecturer, author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. [D]
He married Olivia (Livy) Langdon in 1870; they had a son and three daughters. [D]
Their first child, Langdon, died of diphtheria in 1872, at about two years old. [D]
Bad investments brought him to bankruptcy: his publishing company failed in 1894, and from July 1895 to July 1896 he made a worldwide lecture tour to earn money; he repaid his creditors. [D]
His eldest daughter, Susy, died of meningitis in August 1896, at 24, while staying at the family's former home in Hartford; the family never returned to live in Hartford. [D]

His wife, Olivia, died of heart failure at the Villa di Quarto near Florence, Italy, on the evening of June 5, 1904, after 22 months of illness; in his notebook that night he wrote that "she that was the life of my life" had died. [D]
He had his first attack of gout in Paris in about 1894 and was laid up with gout again in Vienna in October 1897. [D]
On May 18, 1905, he arrived for the summer at a rented house at Dublin, New Hampshire, in the hills below Mount Monadnock. [D]

text.paragraph: 7 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
No medications started by this date.

list.item: Writer, humorist and lecturer for more than forty years; known by his pen name; writing most mornings but unable to finish anything since his wife died [S]

Widowed a year ago after 34 years of marriage; has lost a son in early childhood and a daughter as a young woman; lives in a rented house in the hills for the summer with a family member, a secretary and household staff; no relative is named or given a role in this record [S]

Tobacco: cigars since boyhood, now about fifteen a day and a pipe in the evening, with some smoke inhaled; has stopped for months at a time before and always started again; says cigars help him write [S]
Alcohol: a glass of whisky most evenings (AUDIT-C 3); no other drugs [S]
Finances: lost everything in a business failure about ten years ago and repaid his creditors by lecturing; secure now; still anxious about money at night [S]
No firearms in the house; walks the hill roads most days [S]
Strengths: humor, a lifetime of writing, many friends and admirers, neighbors in the summer colony who visit, a daily routine of work, and his own decision to come in [S]

Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone, means safety, a telephone call in three days, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: Loss of partner and suicide risks among oldest old: a population-based register study (2004); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Tobacco: his readiness asked at every visit; brief advice linked to his own concern about his heart; counseling at each visit and the state quitline; varenicline offered as the most effective single medicine, with combination nicotine replacement as the alternative. Guideline: Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

Chest tightness on exertion: resting ECG today and CT coronary angiography, chosen over stress testing for a man over 65 with stable symptoms and no known coronary disease; call 911 for chest pain at rest or lasting more than fifteen minutes. Guideline: 2021 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain (2021) [S]

Social connection and his writing: one planned social contact a week, a return to morning writing on a set project, and the clinic social worker's list of local groups; meaning and goals to be part of any grief treatment. Guideline: Treatment of complicated grief: a randomized controlled trial (2005) [S]

Gout: urate measured at intake; urate-lowering therapy explained, since two flares in a year make it strongly recommended; he chose to decide after the chest evaluation; call at the first sign of a flare. Guideline: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout (2020) [S]

Cardiovascular risk: blood pressure at each visit and lipids, hemoglobin A1c and kidney function at baseline; prediabetes (hemoglobin A1c 5.8 percent) managed with walking and diet. Guideline: 2021 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]
